title: Electronic configuration (basic)
definition:
Electronic configuration is the way in which electrons are arranged in different shells or energy levels around the nucleus of an atom. The concept is built on the idea that every atom has a central, dense, positively charged nucleus containing protons and neutrons, while the negatively charged electrons occupy the extra nuclear part in well-defined regions called shells. The number of protons in the nucleus is called the atomic number, and in a neutral atom this is exactly equal to the number of electrons. The mass number, on the other hand, is the total number of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus. Because the mass of an electron is negligible compared with that of a proton or neutron, the mass number does not include electrons.

In the elementary model of the atom, the shells are filled in a definite order, starting from the shell nearest the nucleus and moving outward. The first shell, which is the smallest and closest to the nucleus, can hold a maximum of two electrons. The second shell can hold up to eight electrons, and the third shell can also hold up to eight electrons in the first twenty elements. This means that the electronic configuration of the first twenty elements follows a simple pattern: 2 in the first shell, up to 8 in the second, and up to 8 in the third, before the fourth shell begins to receive electrons. For example, hydrogen, with atomic number 1, has a single electron in the first shell and is written as 1. Helium, with atomic number 2, has two electrons in the first shell and is written as 2. Lithium, with atomic number 3, has the configuration 2,1; the first shell is filled with two electrons and the third electron goes into the second shell.

As we move across the first twenty elements, each increase in atomic number adds one more electron to the shells. Oxygen, with atomic number 8, has two electrons in the first shell and six in the second, giving 2,6. Sodium, with atomic number 11, fills the first shell with 2, the second with 8, and the remaining electron occupies the third shell, giving 2,8,1. Argon, with atomic number 18, completes the third shell with 2,8,8. Potassium and calcium begin to place electrons in the fourth shell, giving 2,8,8,1 and 2,8,8,2 respectively. This shell filling pattern is not arbitrary; the first twenty elements always follow the rule that each shell is filled to its maximum before a new shell begins, and because protons and electrons are equal in a neutral atom, the atomic number tells us both how many protons the nucleus has and how many electrons must be arranged in the shells.

The arrangement of electrons in shells is deeply connected to the chemical behaviour of an element. The outermost electrons are the ones that take part in chemical reactions, and the number of electrons in the outermost shell determines the valency of the element. For instance, oxygen with 2,6 has six electrons in its outer shell and tends to gain two electrons to complete eight. Sodium with 2,8,1 has a single electron in its outermost shell and tends to lose it. Calcium with 2,8,8,2 has two electrons in its outermost shell and also tends to lose them. Thus, electronic configuration is not merely a way of counting electrons; it is a model that explains why elements react the way they do. Charts and models showing the structure of the atom, with the nucleus at the centre and electrons in circular or elliptical shells, are commonly used in Class 7 to visualise this arrangement and to make the abstract idea of electron distribution concrete.

In the Indian school context, this topic forms the bridge between the simple particle picture of the atom and the more detailed ideas of periodicity and bonding that come in later classes. A clear grasp of shell filling for the first twenty elements is essential before the student can understand ion formation, valency, or the periodic table. The topic is also important because the ICSE examiner frequently observes that candidates who do not master the basic filling of shells struggle when later questions ask for electronic configurations of ions or when they are asked to explain stability in terms of completely filled outer shells. A strong foundation here therefore has lasting value.
textWalkthrough:
Let us begin with what you already know. In the earlier node c6_chem_010, you met the atom as a tiny particle with a central nucleus and particles called protons, neutrons, and electrons. You learned that the atomic number of an element tells you how many protons are in the nucleus and, in a neutral atom, how many electrons are moving around it. You also learned that the mass number is simply the sum of protons and neutrons. That knowledge is your starting point now. Before we go further, the immediate prerequisite is c7_chem_009, where you studied the properties of the electron: it carries a negative charge and has almost no mass compared with a proton. This is important because the electrons, being lightweight and negatively charged, are held in the extra nuclear part by the attraction of the positive nucleus, and their arrangement in shells explains why atoms behave as they do.

Now, imagine the nucleus as the centre of a series of circular tracks, like the lanes around a school ground. These tracks are the shells, and the electrons are students placed on these tracks. The first track, the one closest to the nucleus, is the smallest and can hold only two students. The second track is larger and can hold eight. The third track can also hold eight for the first twenty elements, and only after these tracks are filled does the fourth track begin to receive electrons. This is the basic shell filling rule. When we write the electronic configuration of an atom, we are simply stating how many electrons are in each track, starting from the innermost one.

Let us take oxygen as our first example. Oxygen has atomic number 8, so a neutral oxygen atom has eight protons in the nucleus and eight electrons around it. The first two electrons go into the first shell, giving 2. The remaining six go into the second shell, giving 6. So the electronic configuration of oxygen is 2,6. A good answer would draw a small circle for the nucleus, write +8 inside it for the protons, and then draw two concentric rings with two dots on the inner ring and six on the outer. A weak answer would simply write 2,6 without any diagram, or worse, write 2,8 without remembering that only eight electrons are available. Another common weak answer is to start with the outer shell and write 6,2, which reverses the order and shows that the student has not understood that shells are filled from the inside out.

Now look at sodium. Sodium has atomic number 11, which means eleven protons and eleven electrons. The first shell takes 2, the second takes 8, and the single remaining electron goes into the third shell. So the electronic configuration is 2,8,1. A strong student will also notice that sodium has only one electron in its outermost shell and will connect this to the fact that sodium tends to lose one electron in chemical reactions. A weaker student might write 2,8,1 correctly but fail to explain that the outermost electron is the one responsible for the reaction. The best answers always connect the arrangement to the behaviour of the element.

Calcium is the last of the first twenty elements and is an excellent example because it has four shells. With atomic number 20, calcium has twenty electrons. The first shell takes 2, the second takes 8, the third takes 8, and the remaining 2 go into the fourth shell. Thus calcium has the electronic configuration 2,8,8,2. A correct diagram will show the four shells, and a good student will point out that the outermost shell has two electrons, which calcium can lose. A weak answer here often confuses the order and writes something like 2,8,2,8 or 2,2,8,8, which makes it appear as though there are two electrons in the second shell before the third is full. Remember, each shell is filled to its limit before the next one starts, except that the third shell in the first twenty elements also stops at eight.

When you draw charts and models, try to be neat. The nucleus is small and dense; the extra nuclear part is the space around it. Place the electrons as dots on the shells, and write the numbers clearly below the diagram as 2, 8, 8, and so on. Teachers often prefer the number form to the dot form because it is unambiguous, but the dot form helps you visualise the arrangement. Use both: draw the dot diagram, then write the numbers to confirm it.

Let us now think about what the ICSE board exam expects. Examiners expect you to write the electronic configuration of the first twenty elements accurately and to relate the configuration to atomic number and mass number. They also expect you to use charts or models to show the arrangement. The board examiner observations repeatedly point out that many candidates who attempt electronic configuration questions forget the basic idea that half-filled and completely filled shells are more stable than incomplete arrangements. While that deeper point belongs to later classes, the seed is planted here: an outermost shell with eight electrons, like that of neon or argon, is a very stable arrangement, and elements try to reach such a state by gaining, losing, or sharing electrons. You should therefore remember that shell filling is not just a counting exercise; it is the first step in understanding why some elements are reactive and others are not.

misconceptionText:
Misconception 1 -- Writing electronic configuration without knowing the atomic number: board examiners have observed that even when the atomic number is given, many candidates are unable to write the correct electronic configuration. The correction is simple: the atomic number equals the number of protons and, in a neutral atom, equals the number of electrons. Start with that number and distribute the electrons as 2, then 8, then 8, then more.

Misconception 2 -- Confusing the order of shells: Some students write the configuration from the outer shell inwards, such as 6,2 for oxygen instead of 2,6. This shows a misunderstanding that shells must be filled from the nucleus outward. The correct method is to place the first 2 electrons in the first shell, the next 8 in the second, and so on, and to write the numbers in the same order: K, L, M, N.

Misconception 3 -- Forgetting that a completely filled outer shell is stable: The board examiner observations note that candidates often fail to mention that half-filled and completely filled orbitals or shells are more stable. In Class 7, the key idea is that an outermost shell of 8 electrons is a stable arrangement. This is why noble gases like neon and argon are unreactive. When answering, always note whether the configuration ends in a complete or incomplete outer shell.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): Define atomic number and mass number. How are these numbers related to the electronic configuration of a neutral atom?
Answer: The atomic number of an element is the number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom. It is represented by the symbol Z. In a neutral atom, the number of protons is exactly equal to the number of electrons, because the positive charge of the protons is balanced by the negative charge of the electrons. The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus. It is represented by the symbol A and does not include electrons because the mass of an electron is negligible compared with that of a proton or a neutron. The relation to electronic configuration is direct: since the atomic number tells us the number of electrons in a neutral atom, it tells us how many electrons must be arranged in shells around the nucleus. For example, an oxygen atom with atomic number 8 has eight electrons, which are arranged as 2,6. A sodium atom with atomic number 11 has eleven electrons, arranged as 2,8,1. Thus, once the atomic number is known, the electronic configuration can be worked out by placing two electrons in the first shell, up to eight in the second, and so on. The mass number does not change the electronic configuration, but it is useful for finding the number of neutrons by subtracting the atomic number from it.

Q2 (reasoning): Sulphur has atomic number 16. Explain how you would distribute its sixteen electrons into shells and write its electronic configuration.
Answer: Since sulphur has atomic number 16, a neutral sulphur atom has sixteen protons in its nucleus and sixteen electrons in the extra nuclear part. To write the electronic configuration, I would place the electrons in shells starting from the one nearest the nucleus. The first shell can hold a maximum of two electrons, so the first two electrons go there, giving 2. This leaves fourteen electrons. The second shell can hold a maximum of eight electrons, so the next eight go into the second shell, giving 8. This leaves six electrons. The third shell can hold up to eight electrons for the first twenty elements, so the remaining six electrons go into the third shell. Therefore, the electronic configuration of sulphur is 2,8,6. The first and second shells are completely filled, while the third shell has six electrons and is incomplete. Because the outermost shell has six electrons, sulphur tends to gain two electrons to complete its octet and become stable. It is important not to write 2,6,8 or 2,8,8, because there are only sixteen electrons in total and the shells must be filled from the inside out.

Q3 (evaluate): A student says, "The mass number of an atom is always greater than its atomic number, so the mass number tells us more about how the electrons are arranged in shells than the atomic number does." Evaluate this statement.
Answer: The student's statement is partly correct in one respect but incorrect overall. It is true that the mass number is usually greater than the atomic number, because the mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons while the atomic number is only the number of protons. For hydrogen-1, the mass number is 1 and the atomic number is 1, so they can be equal, but for every other element the mass number is larger. However, the second part of the statement is wrong. The mass number does not tell us how the electrons are arranged in shells. The number of electrons is determined by the atomic number, not the mass number. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, which is the atomic number. The mass number includes neutrons, which are in the nucleus and have no effect on the electron arrangement. Therefore, to find the electronic configuration, we use the atomic number, not the mass number. For example, carbon has atomic number 6 and mass number 12. The 6 tells us there are six electrons to arrange as 2,4, while the 12 only tells us that there are also six neutrons. The student has mixed up the roles of these two numbers. A better statement would be: the atomic number determines the number of electrons and hence the electronic configuration, while the mass number tells us the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

Q4 (apply): A magnesium atom has atomic number 12 and mass number 24. Draw a labelled diagram of the atom showing the nucleus and the electron shells, and write the electronic configuration. How many protons, neutrons, and electrons are present?
Answer: Magnesium has atomic number 12, which means it has 12 protons in the nucleus. Since the atom is neutral, it also has 12 electrons. The mass number is 24, so the number of neutrons is the mass number minus the atomic number, which is 24 - 12 = 12 neutrons. The electronic configuration is found by distributing the 12 electrons in shells. The first shell takes 2 electrons, the second shell takes 8 electrons, and the remaining 2 electrons go into the third shell. So the electronic configuration is 2,8,2. In a labelled diagram, I would draw a small circle at the centre and label it "nucleus: 12 protons + 12 neutrons, charge +12" or simply write 12p, 12n inside it. Around the nucleus I would draw three concentric shells. The innermost shell would have 2 dots or electrons, the second shell 8 dots, and the third shell 2 dots. Below or beside the diagram I would write the configuration as 2,8,2. A common mistake is to draw 2,8,1 and say there are 11 electrons, which would be a magnesium ion, not a neutral atom. Another mistake is to put 24 electrons because the student confuses the mass number with the electron count. The correct answer is 12 protons, 12 neutrons, and 12 electrons, with configuration 2,8,2.

Q5 (create): Design a simple teaching chart or model that a Class 7 student can use to remember the shell filling pattern for the first twenty elements. Your chart must include at least three examples from the syllabus: oxygen, sodium, and calcium.
Answer: I would design a wall chart titled "Electron Shells for the First Twenty Elements." The chart would have a large central circle representing the nucleus, with four concentric rings around it representing the K, L, M, and N shells. At the top of the chart, I would write the rule: "Fill each shell from the inside. K holds 2, L holds 8, M holds 8, then N begins." On the left side, I would list the first twenty elements with their atomic numbers. The three examples would be shown clearly in colour. For oxygen, I would draw the nucleus with +8 inside, the K shell with 2 blue dots, and the L shell with 6 blue dots, with the number 2,6 written below. I would add a short note: "Oxygen has 6 electrons in its outer shell and needs 2 more to be stable." For sodium, the nucleus would have +11, with 2, 8, and 1 green dot in the K, L, and M shells, and the configuration 2,8,1 written below. The note would say: "Sodium has 1 outer electron and tends to lose it." For calcium, the nucleus would have +20, with 2, 8, 8, and 2 red dots in the K, L, M, and N shells, and the configuration 2,8,8,2 below. The note would say: "Calcium has 2 outer electrons and also tends to lose them." To make the chart interactive, I would include a blank atom template at the bottom where students can use stickers to place electrons and then write the configuration. This hands-on model would help visual learners remember that each shell has a limit and that the outermost electrons determine how the element behaves.
masteryCriteria: Can state the rules for filling electron shells (2, 8, 8, then 18); can write the electronic configuration for elements 1-20 (e.g., Na: 2,8,1; Cl: 2,8,7); can state the relationship between valence electrons and valency.

title: Valency
definition:
Valency is the combining capacity of an element -- it tells us how many atoms of another element, especially hydrogen, can combine with one atom of the given element. Because one atom of hydrogen can form just one bond, we treat the hydrogen atom as the standard unit of measurement for this combining capacity. If one atom of an element combines with one hydrogen atom, the element is monovalent; if it combines with two, it is divalent; with three, trivalent; and with four, tetravalent. This is why sodium is monovalent, oxygen is divalent, nitrogen and aluminium are trivalent, and carbon and silicon are tetravalent.

At a deeper level, the valency of an element is determined by its electronic configuration, and more specifically by the number of electrons present in the outermost shell of its atom. These outermost electrons are called valence electrons. In a metallic element such as sodium, magnesium or aluminium, the valency is usually equal to the number of valence electrons, because the atom can lose those electrons to attain a stable outermost shell. Sodium has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 1, so it has one valence electron in its outermost shell and its valency is one. Magnesium is 2, 8, 2, so its valency is two. Aluminium is 2, 8, 3, so its valency is three.

For non-metallic elements such as oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine, the valency is often the number of electrons the atom must gain or share to complete an octet -- that is, to have eight electrons in its outermost shell. Oxygen, with the electronic configuration 2, 6, needs two more electrons to complete its octet, so its valency is two. Nitrogen, with 2, 5, needs three electrons, so it can be trivalent. Carbon, with 2, 4, needs four more electrons, but in the language of hydrogen combination it behaves as tetravalent because it forms four bonds, as in methane, CH4. Chlorine, with 2, 8, 7, needs only one electron to complete its octet, so it is monovalent.

Valency is not restricted to individual elements; it also applies to radicals or groups of atoms that behave as single units in chemical reactions and carry a definite charge. A radical has a combining capacity of its own, which is the same as the magnitude of the charge it carries but with the opposite sign. Thus the sulphate radical, SO4, carries two negative charges, so it is divalent. The carbonate radical, CO3, also carries two negative charges, so it is divalent. The nitrate radical, NO3, carries one negative charge, so it is monovalent. The hydroxide radical, OH, also carries one negative charge, so it is monovalent.

Once the valencies of the elements or radicals in a compound are known, the formula of the compound can be derived. The guiding principle is that in a neutral compound the total positive valency must equal the total negative valency. If an element A has valency x and another element or radical B has valency y, then the simplest formula is A_yB_x when x and y are whole numbers. For example, aluminium is trivalent and the sulphate radical is divalent, so the formula of aluminium sulphate is Al2(SO4)3. Two atoms of aluminium contribute a total positive valency of six, and three sulphate radicals contribute a total negative valency of six, so the compound is electrically balanced.

In short, valency is the bridge between the electronic structure of an atom and the formulas of the compounds it can form. It is a practical concept that grows out of the idea of the outermost shell and the drive of every atom to achieve a stable octet, either by losing, gaining or sharing electrons.
textWalkthrough:
Let us begin by recalling what you already know. In the earlier node c6_chem_009, you learned that valency is the combining capacity of an element -- a simple idea that describes how many hydrogen atoms can join hands with one atom of that element. You saw examples such as sodium combining with one hydrogen to form NaH, oxygen with two to form H2O, and carbon with four to form CH4. That understanding is the seed from which today's lesson grows.

Now, in c7_chem_011, we are going to connect that seed to a deeper root: the arrangement of electrons around the nucleus. Your direct prerequisite is c7_chem_010, where you studied electronic configuration -- the systematic distribution of electrons in shells, like K, L, M and so on. You learned that the electrons in the outermost shell are special because they are the ones that participate in chemical bonding. The number of these valence electrons decides how an atom will behave when it meets another atom. This is why a child must know electronic configuration before understanding valency: the shell arrangement directly defines how many bonds an atom can form.

Imagine an atom as a busy traveller carrying a bag of electrons. The electrons in the outermost pocket of the bag are the easiest to give away, the easiest to receive, or the easiest to share. If the atom is a metal, it tends to empty that outermost pocket by giving away electrons. Sodium has one electron in its outermost shell, so it gives away one electron and its valency is one. Magnesium has two, so it gives away two and its valency is two. Aluminium has three, so its valency is three. Notice the pattern: for metals, valency is simply the number of electrons in the outermost shell.

But what if the atom is a non-metal? Then it usually tries to fill its outermost shell to the magic number of eight, which we call the octet. Oxygen has six electrons in its outermost shell, so it needs two more to make eight; therefore its valency is two. Nitrogen has five, so it needs three, and its valency is three. Carbon has four, and in the world of hydrogen it combines with four atoms, so its valency is four. Chlorine has seven, and it needs just one more electron to complete its octet, so it is monovalent. The same logic runs through all of these examples: valency is about the tendency to reach a stable outermost shell.

Let us now look at radicals, which are groups of atoms that stick together and behave like one charged passenger. A radical has its own combining capacity, which is equal to the magnitude of its charge. If the radical has one unit of negative charge, it can combine with one unit of positive valency, so it is monovalent. The nitrate radical NO3 and the hydroxide radical OH are of this kind. If the radical has two units of negative charge, it is divalent and can satisfy two units of positive valency. The sulphate radical SO4 and the carbonate radical CO3 are divalent. Understanding this is crucial because it lets you write formulas for compounds such as sodium sulphate, magnesium nitrate and aluminium carbonate.

When you write the formula of a compound, always ask yourself whether the total positive valency equals the total negative valency. This is the heart of correct formula derivation. For example, if you join aluminium, which is trivalent, with the sulphate radical, which is divalent, you need two aluminium atoms to give a total positive valency of six and three sulphate radicals to give a total negative valency of six. The formula is therefore Al2(SO4)3. This is a good answer: it uses the valencies correctly and the compound is electrically neutral. A weak answer would simply swap the numbers and write Al3(SO4)2, which is not balanced and would lose marks.

Another good-versus-bad comparison concerns electronic configuration. A good response to "Determine the valency of oxygen" states: "Oxygen has the electronic configuration 2, 6, so it has six valence electrons. It needs two more electrons to complete its octet, so its valency is two." A weak response merely writes "Oxygen has six valence electrons" without explaining how that gives the valency or without mentioning the octet. Always show the reasoning.

Let us close with what the ICSE board exam expects from you. The examiner wants to see that you can relate the number of valence electrons to valency, that you can determine valency for both elements and radicals, and that you can use valency to derive simple formulas. The board exam guidance remind teachers to focus on the relationship between the number of valence electrons and the group or period, and to train students to follow the letters or instructions given in the question. So read every question carefully: if the paper gives symbols or letters, use those symbols; do not replace them with names. Show the electronic configuration, mention the outermost shell, and connect it directly to the valency. If you do that, your answer will be complete and precise.

Misconception 1: Some students write only the electronic configuration and stop, without explaining how the outermost shell electrons give the valency. Examiners have noticed that candidates often give the electronic configuration of an ion but do not explain the concept of paired and unpaired electrons or the d-d transition behind it; in a similar way, at this level, listing shells is not enough. You must go one step further and say how the number of valence electrons leads to the combining capacity. The correction is to complete the sentence: "The atom has ... electrons in its outermost shell, therefore it can lose, gain or share ... electrons, so its valency is ..."

Misconception 2: Some candidates write the name or symbol of the element when the question specifically asks them to use the given letters. The examiner comment for the 2020 paper observed that many candidates identified the elements instead of choosing the given alphabets and that teachers should train students to use the letters given in the question. The correction is to read the instruction line carefully: if the question gives letters such as A, B, C or X, Y, Z, use those letters in your answer, not the real element names, unless the question asks for them.

Misconception 3: A common error in formula writing is to place the subscripts in the wrong order or to forget that the compound must be electrically neutral. For example, a student might write MgOH for magnesium hydroxide because magnesium is divalent and the hydroxide radical is monovalent. The correct formula is Mg(OH)2, because one magnesium atom provides two positive valencies and each hydroxide radical provides one negative valency, so you need two hydroxide radicals to balance the charge.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): Define valency and explain how it is related to the number of electrons in the outermost shell of an atom.
Answer: Valency is the combining capacity of an element -- the number of hydrogen atoms that can combine with one atom of the element. It is also the number of electrons that an atom can lose, gain or share in order to complete its outermost shell, usually to reach the stable octet of eight electrons. The number of electrons present in the outermost shell of an atom is called the number of valence electrons, and this number is the key to determining the valency. For example, sodium has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 1, which means that it has one electron in its outermost shell. Because it is a metal, it can lose that one electron and leave a stable octet in the next inner shell, so its valency is one. Magnesium has the configuration 2, 8, 2, so it loses two electrons and its valency is two. On the other hand, oxygen has the configuration 2, 6, so it has six valence electrons. Being a non-metal, it gains or shares two electrons to complete its octet, so its valency is two. In this way, the outermost shell acts like a little workshop where the actual business of combining with other atoms is decided. The number of electrons in this workshop tells us how many hands the atom can lend to other atoms, and that number is the valency.

Q2 (reasoning): Why are the noble gases helium, neon and argon usually said to have zero valency?
Answer: The valency of an element depends on its ability to lose, gain or share electrons in order to achieve a stable outermost shell. Noble gases such as helium, neon and argon have completely filled outermost shells. Helium has two electrons in its only shell, which is the maximum that shell can hold, so it is already stable. Neon has the configuration 2, 8, with eight electrons in its outermost shell, and argon has the configuration 2, 8, 8, also with a complete octet in its outermost shell. Because their outermost shells are already full, these atoms do not need to lose, gain or share any electrons. They do not try to combine with hydrogen or with other atoms under ordinary conditions, which is why they are called inert or noble gases. Since there is no tendency to form a bond, their combining capacity is zero, and we say that their valency is zero. This is the reason noble gases are placed at the far right of the periodic table and are used as a reference for the stable octet that other atoms try to achieve.

Q3 (evaluate): A student says, "An element with seven electrons in its outermost shell has valency 7 because it has seven valence electrons." Evaluate this statement.
Answer: This statement is not fully correct, and it shows an incomplete understanding of the way valency is determined. The statement correctly notes that the element has seven valence electrons, but it wrongly concludes that the valency is seven. In the study of chemical bonding, valency is the number of electrons an atom can lose, gain or share in order to reach a stable outermost shell. For most small atoms, the stable shell contains eight electrons, which is called the octet. If an element already has seven electrons in its outermost shell, it needs only one more electron to complete the octet. Therefore its tendency is to gain one electron, not to lose seven or share all seven. The valency of such an element is therefore one, not seven. A good example is chlorine, whose electronic configuration is 2, 8, 7. Chlorine is a non-metal and it gains one electron to form the chloride ion Cl-, or it shares one electron to form one covalent bond as in hydrogen chloride, HCl. In both cases the combining capacity with hydrogen or with a monovalent metal is one. However, there is a small sense in which the statement could be defended for very large atoms: in the case of some heavier elements, the number of outermost electrons can sometimes suggest a higher positive valency when the atom loses several electrons, but that is not the situation we consider in Class 7. For the elements you will meet in this course, valency for a non-metal with seven valence electrons is one. So the statement should be rejected as an over-simplification.

Q4 (apply): An element X has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 3. It combines with the sulphate radical SO4. Determine the valency of X, the valency of SO4, and write the correct formula of the compound formed.
Answer: To solve this, we first look at the outermost shell of element X. Its electronic configuration is 2, 8, 3, which tells us that it has three electrons in its outermost shell. Since X is a metal, it can lose these three electrons to achieve a stable octet in the shell below, so the valency of X is three and it is a trivalent element. This pattern matches aluminium, which has the same configuration. Next, the sulphate radical SO4 is a group of atoms that carries two negative charges, because the sulphur and four oxygen atoms together have accepted two extra electrons to form the ion SO4^2-. The combining capacity, or valency, of a radical is the same as the magnitude of its charge, so the valency of the sulphate radical is two and it is divalent. To write the formula of the compound, we use the crisscross or balancing method. The total positive valency supplied by X must equal the total negative valency supplied by SO4. Since X is trivalent and SO4 is divalent, the least common multiple of three and two is six. Therefore we need two atoms of X to give a total positive valency of 2 x 3 = 6, and we need three sulphate radicals to give a total negative valency of 3 x 2 = 6. The correct formula is X2(SO4)3. If X is identified as aluminium, the formula is Al2(SO4)3, which is aluminium sulphate, a compound you often see in school laboratories and in water treatment in Indian towns. The important point is that the overall charge on the compound is zero, because the positive and negative valencies balance each other exactly.

Q5 (create): Design a classroom game called "Valency Match" that helps students remember the valencies of common elements and radicals. Explain the rules and two sample rounds.
Answer: The game "Valency Match" is played in pairs or small groups and uses a set of cards. Half of the cards show elements or radicals, such as Na, Mg, Al, C, O, Cl, SO4, NO3, CO3 and OH, and the other half show matching numbers or descriptions of valency, such as "monovalent", "divalent", "trivalent" and "tetravalent". The cards are shuffled and placed face down. Players take turns flipping one element card and one valency card. If the valency card correctly describes the element or radical on the basis of its electronic configuration or charge, the player keeps the pair and earns one point. For example, if a player turns over the Na card and the "monovalent" card, the match is correct because sodium has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 1, giving it one valence electron and a valency of one. If a player turns over the SO4 card and the "divalent" card, the match is correct because the sulphate radical has a charge of 2-. In a more advanced version, after making a correct match the player must also explain the reason: "Sodium is monovalent because it has one electron in its outermost shell, which it can lose to complete an octet." A sample second round might involve Mg and the "divalent" card; the player would explain that magnesium has the configuration 2, 8, 2, so it loses two electrons and has valency two. To make the game Indian, the cards could also include everyday substances such as common salt from Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan, limestone from Madhya Pradesh, or baking soda used in kitchens, and the players could be asked to name the compound formula. The game helps students move quickly from memorising a list to explaining the underlying rule that valency depends on the outermost shell.

title: Language of chemistry - chemical equations
definition: The language of chemistry is built from a few powerful tools. A symbol is a short form for an element, usually one or two letters taken from its name: H for hydrogen, O for oxygen, Na for sodium, Cl for chlorine, Fe for iron, Cu for copper, and so on. The first twenty elements are especially important because they appear again and again in everyday substances. A formula is the chemist's way of showing which atoms are joined in a compound and in what ratio. The formula is decided by valency -- the combining capacity of an atom. For example, hydrogen has a valency of 1 and oxygen has a valency of 2, so water is written H_2O; sodium has a valency of 1 and chlorine has a valency of 1, so sodium chloride is NaCl. A word equation lists reactants and products in words, such as "hydrogen + oxygen -> water." A chemical equation does the same thing using symbols and formulae: 2H_2(g) + O_2(g) -> 2H_2O(l). The arrow means "produces" or "gives," and the substances on the left are the reactants while those on the right are the products. Balancing means adjusting the numbers in front of the formulae -- called coefficients -- so that every type of atom is the same on both sides. This is demanded by the law of conservation of mass, which says that matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. If you start with four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms, you must end with the same count. The process of balancing is like keeping a seesaw level: both pans must hold equal total "atom weight." State symbols are often written in brackets after each formula: (s) for solid, (l) for liquid, (g) for gas, and (aq) for a substance dissolved in water. A chemical equation gives rich information -- the reactants, the products, their formulae, the number of molecules or moles, and, through state symbols, the physical state. But it also has clear limitations. A chemical equation does not, by itself, tell us whether a catalyst is needed, what temperature or pressure is required, the speed at which the reaction occurs, or whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. In short, it is like a labelled recipe: it shows ingredients and results in exact amounts, but it does not show the oven temperature, the cooking time, or the special bowl that makes the process work. Understanding these boundaries helps a student use chemical equations correctly and avoid the common trap of treating the equation as the complete story of the reaction.
textWalkthrough:
Let us begin by looking back at what you already know. In the earlier node c6_chem_012, you learned to write word equations and to build compound formulae. That means you can already take a sentence such as "calcium carbonate gives calcium oxide and carbon dioxide on heating" and rewrite it as a word equation: calcium carbonate -> calcium oxide + carbon dioxide. You also learned that formulae depend on valency. That idea is the bridge we now cross. In this node, c7_chem_012, we move from word equations to full chemical equations by using symbols, formulae, and the law of conservation of mass.

Before we can do that, we need a direct skill from the prerequisite node c7_chem_011: valency. Valency is simply the number of bonds an atom can form, or its combining capacity. Why is it so important? Because every formula in a chemical equation is determined by valency. If you do not know that magnesium has a valency of 2 and oxygen has a valency of 2, you might write MgO_2 instead of MgO for magnesium oxide. If you do not know that hydrogen is monovalent, you cannot decide whether the product of zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid is ZnCl or ZnCl_2. So the first thing to do before drawing any chemical equation is to recall the valencies of the elements involved. Keep a small table of valencies for the first twenty elements handy; it is one of the most useful tools in chemistry.

Now let us look at the steps for changing a word equation into a balanced chemical equation. Step one is to identify the reactants and products and write their correct formulae using valency. Step two is to place the reactants on the left and the products on the right, connected by an arrow. Step three is to count every kind of atom on both sides. Step four is to add coefficients in front of the formulae -- never change the subscripts inside a formula, because that would change the identity of the substance -- until the number of each type of atom is the same on both sides. The final equation must show the same total number of each kind of atom before and after the reaction.

Let us take a very Indian example. When you heat white marble chips, which are mainly calcium carbonate and can be obtained from the famous marble quarries near Makrana in Rajasthan, the product is quicklime, calcium oxide, and a gas, carbon dioxide. The word equation is: calcium carbonate -> calcium oxide + carbon dioxide. Using symbols, we get CaCO_3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO_2(g). Count the atoms: on the left, one calcium, one carbon, three oxygen; on the right, one calcium, one carbon, and in the products together, one oxygen plus two oxygen, which is three oxygen. The equation is already balanced. This is a GOOD example because every atom is accounted for and the state symbols are included.

A BAD example would be to write CaCO_3 -> CaO + CO_2 with no state symbols, because a learner might think the marble is a liquid or the carbon dioxide is a solid. An even worse example is to change the formula to CaCO_2 in an attempt to balance, which creates a substance that does not exist. The rule is: coefficients can change, subscripts cannot.

Here is another example. Hydrogen gas burns in oxygen to form water, a reaction you can show with a small squeaky-pop test in the school laboratory. The unbalanced equation is H_2(g) + O_2(g) -> H_2O(l). Counting atoms gives two hydrogen and two oxygen on the left, but only two hydrogen and one oxygen on the right. To balance the oxygen, we place a 2 in front of H_2O: H_2 + O_2 -> 2H_2O. Now the right side has four hydrogen atoms, so we put a 2 in front of H_2 on the left: 2H_2(g) + O_2(g) -> 2H_2O(l). Count again: four hydrogen and two oxygen on each side. This is balanced.

The reason we can balance equations at all is the law of conservation of mass. This law says that the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. No atom disappears, and no new atom is created. In our hydrogen-oxygen example, four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms before the reaction are still four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms after the reaction. They are simply rearranged into water molecules. This is why a balanced chemical equation is like a tightly kept account book: every atom must be present on both the debit and the credit side.

Once an equation is balanced and state symbols are added, what information does it give? It tells us the reactants and products, their formulae, the relative numbers of molecules or moles taking part, and the physical state of each substance at the time of reaction. But it also has limitations. The equation does not tell us whether a catalyst is used. A catalyst is a substance that changes the speed of a reaction without being consumed, but it is not a reactant or a product, so it appears above the arrow, not in the main equation. The equation does not tell us the conditions: is the reaction heated? Is it carried out under pressure? Is light or electricity needed? It does not tell us whether the reaction is fast or slow, hot or cold, safe or dangerous. board examiners have repeatedly noticed that students confuse reagents and conditions and forget to show catalysts or specific states. For instance, when candidates are asked to write equations, some omit the state symbols or write wrong reactants because they have not understood the conditions of the laboratory preparation. The equation itself is clean, but the story around it is not.

When you face board questions, expect a word equation to be given and you may be asked to convert it into a balanced chemical equation, or a chemical equation may be given and you may be asked to add state symbols or explain what information it gives. Examiners like to test whether you understand the difference between a balanced equation and a complete description of the reaction. So practise writing equations for the first twenty elements, keep the law of conservation of mass in mind, and always ask yourself: "Are the number of atoms equal on both sides, and what does this equation not tell me?"

Misconception 1: "If I write the correct formulae, the equation is automatically balanced."
board examiners have noticed that many candidates are unable to write correct balanced chemical equations, often getting the reactants and products confused. Writing correct formulae is only the beginning. Even with the right formulae, the number of atoms of each element may not match on both sides. The correction is to count each type of atom after writing the skeleton equation and then add coefficients. For example, H_2(g) + O_2(g) -> H_2O(l) has correct formulae but is not balanced; it must be 2H_2(g) + O_2(g) -> 2H_2O(l).

Misconception 2: "The catalyst should be written on the left-hand side as a reactant or on the right-hand side as a product."

A catalyst is not consumed in the reaction, so it is not placed in the main equation as a reactant or product. Instead, it is written above or below the arrow. For example, the decomposition of potassium chlorate is written 2KClO_3(s) ->[MnO_2] 2KCl(s) + 3O_2(g), with the catalyst MnO_2 shown separately. Conditions such as heat (Delta) are also written above or below the arrow.

Misconception 3: "A balanced chemical equation tells us everything about the reaction, including speed, conditions, and safety."
This is a frequent error. board examiners have observed that students give incomplete descriptions of reactions because they forget the limitations of an equation. The equation tells us what reacts, what forms, and the relative amounts, but it does not tell us the temperature, pressure, catalyst, or how fast the reaction happens. For instance, the equation C(s) + O_2(g) -> CO_2(g) does not tell us that the carbon must be heated to ignite or that the reaction releases a lot of heat.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): Define a chemical equation and list the main pieces of information it can provide about a reaction.
Answer: A chemical equation is a short, symbolic statement that describes a chemical reaction using the symbols of elements and the formulae of compounds. The substances that take part in the reaction are called the reactants and are written on the left-hand side of the arrow. The new substances formed are called the products and are written on the right-hand side. A chemical equation can provide several important pieces of information. It shows which elements or compounds are reacting and which are being produced. It shows the correct formulae of all substances involved. The numbers placed in front of the formulae, called coefficients, tell us the relative numbers of molecules or moles of each substance. When state symbols are included, the equation also tells us whether each substance is a solid (s), a liquid (l), a gas (g), or an aqueous solution (aq). For example, the equation 2H_2(g) + O_2(g) -> 2H_2O(l) tells us that two molecules of hydrogen gas combine with one molecule of oxygen gas to give two molecules of liquid water. However, the equation does not tell us that heat is needed to start the reaction or that a spark may be required; it only tells us the chemical identity and relative amounts of the substances. In this way, the chemical equation is a compact but very useful summary of a reaction.

Q2 (reasoning): Explain why a chemical equation must be balanced, and connect this requirement to the law of conservation of mass.
Answer: A chemical equation must be balanced because it has to show what actually happens during a chemical reaction. In any chemical change, the atoms of the reactants are rearranged to form the products, but no atoms are created or destroyed. This is the law of conservation of mass, which states that the total mass of the reactants is always equal to the total mass of the products. If an equation is not balanced, it would appear that some atoms have appeared from nowhere or have disappeared, which is impossible. Balancing is therefore a way of obeying this law on paper. For example, if we write the unbalanced equation H_2 + O_2 -> H_2O, the left side has two hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms, while the right side has two hydrogen atoms and only one oxygen atom. That would suggest one oxygen atom has vanished, which contradicts the law of conservation of mass. By writing 2H_2 + O_2 -> 2H_2O, we show four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on the left, and the same number on the right. The total mass is conserved because the same number and type of atoms appear on both sides. Balancing also helps us calculate the exact amounts of reactants and products in a laboratory or industrial setting.

Q3 (evaluate): "A balanced chemical equation tells us whether a catalyst is used, the conditions under which the reaction occurs, the speed of the reaction, and the physical states of the reactants and products." Evaluate this statement with a balanced argument.
Answer: This statement is partly true but also partly false, and a careful student must be able to separate the two parts. It is true that a chemical equation, when written with state symbols, tells us the physical states of the reactants and products: solid (s), liquid (l), gas (g), or aqueous (aq). For example, in the equation CaCO_3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO_2(g), the state symbols make it clear that marble or limestone, a solid, gives a solid residue and a gaseous product. The equation also tells us the identities and the relative amounts of reactants and products. However, the statement is false in claiming that the equation tells us about the catalyst, conditions, and speed. A catalyst, such as manganese dioxide in the decomposition of potassium chlorate or iron in the Haber process, is usually written above or below the arrow, not as part of the main equation. Conditions such as temperature, pressure, or the presence of light are also written above or below the arrow, not shown by the coefficients or state symbols. For instance, 2KClO_3(s) ->[MnO_2, Delta] 2KCl(s) + 3O_2(g) shows that a catalyst and heat are needed, but the main equation itself does not reveal this unless it is annotated. The speed of the reaction, whether it is fast or slow, explosive or gentle, is not shown at all. Therefore, a balanced chemical equation is a powerful but limited tool. It is like a recipe card that lists ingredients and quantities but does not mention the oven temperature or how long to bake. Students must learn both what the equation shows and what it does not show.

Q4 (apply): Convert the following word equation into a balanced chemical equation with state symbols, and explain what information the equation gives: zinc + dilute hydrochloric acid -> zinc chloride + hydrogen.
Answer: To convert the word equation into a balanced chemical equation, first write the correct formulae using valency. Zinc is a metal with valency 2, and chlorine with valency 1 gives ZnCl_2. Hydrogen is a diatomic molecule, H_2, and hydrochloric acid is HCl. Dilute hydrochloric acid means HCl dissolved in water, so it is an aqueous solution. The unbalanced equation is Zn(s) + HCl(aq) -> ZnCl_2(aq) + H_2(g). On the left, we have one zinc, one hydrogen, and one chlorine. On the right, we have one zinc, two chlorine, and two hydrogen. To balance, place a 2 in front of HCl on the left: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> ZnCl_2(aq) + H_2(g). Now there is one zinc on each side, two hydrogen on each side, and two chlorine on each side. The equation is balanced. This equation tells us that one atom of solid zinc reacts with two molecules of hydrochloric acid in aqueous solution to give one formula unit of zinc chloride in solution and one molecule of hydrogen gas. The state symbols are important: hydrogen escapes as bubbles of gas, which is why the reaction is used in the school laboratory to prepare small amounts of hydrogen. The equation also tells us the relative amounts: 1 mole of zinc needs 2 moles of HCl to produce 1 mole of zinc chloride and 1 mole of hydrogen. It does not tell us that the reaction is fastest with dilute acid at room temperature or that the zinc must be clean; those are practical conditions that must be learned separately.

Q5 (create): Imagine you are a laboratory assistant preparing a display board for Class 7 students. Design a short, labelled chemical equation that shows the combustion of methane in a Bunsen burner, and write a brief note explaining what the equation can and cannot tell a student about the reaction.
Answer: A suitable display equation for the combustion of methane is CH_4(g) + 2O_2(g) -> CO_2(g) + 2H_2O(l). To make it student-friendly, the board can show little drawings of a Bunsen burner flame on the left and of carbon dioxide and water droplets on the right. Above the arrow, the word "burning" or "ignite" can be written, with a small note that a flame is needed to start the reaction. The balanced equation can be broken down as follows. Start with one molecule of methane gas, CH_4, which is the fuel in a Bunsen burner. Add two molecules of oxygen gas, O_2, from the air. The products are one molecule of carbon dioxide gas, CO_2, and two molecules of water, H_2O, which may condense as a liquid on a cool surface. The equation is balanced because there is one carbon on each side, four hydrogen on each side, and four oxygen on each side. What the equation tells the student: it shows the fuel, the gas needed from the air, and the substances produced. It shows the relative amounts in terms of molecules or moles, and the state symbols show that the reactants are gases and that water forms as a liquid when it cools. What the equation cannot tell the student: it does not show that a flame or spark is needed to begin the reaction; it does not show that the reaction releases heat and light; it does not show that the Bunsen burner's air hole must be adjusted to give a blue flame; and it does not tell us the speed of combustion or the safety precautions needed. The display should therefore be a balanced chemical equation in the centre, with two side panels titled "Information from the equation" and "What the equation does not show."
masteryCriteria: Can write a balanced chemical equation given reactants and products (e.g., 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O); can balance five simple equations by adjusting coefficients; can state the law of conservation of mass as applied to chemical equations.

title: Electronic configuration and valency
definition: The heart of this section is the idea that an atom is not a chaotic swarm of particles but a tiny solar system of shells, with each shell holding a definite maximum number of electrons. Electronic configuration is the precise way in which the electrons of an atom are arranged in these shells, written as a set of numbers such as 2, 8, 1 for sodium or 2, 6 for oxygen. In the first twenty elements, the shells fill in the order K, L, M, N, where the K-shell holds at most two electrons, the L-shell holds at most eight, the M-shell also holds at most eight for the elements we study, and the N-shell begins to receive electrons from potassium and calcium onward. Valency is the combining capacity of an element, the number of electrons an atom can lose, gain, or share when it joins with other atoms to form a molecule or a compound. Because the outermost shell, also called the valence shell, is the one that takes part in bonding, the number of electrons in that shell decides the valency. When the outermost shell has one, two, three, or four electrons, the atom usually gives away or shares those electrons, so the valency is equal to that count, as in sodium with 2, 8, 1 giving valency 1 or carbon with 2, 4 giving valency 4. When the outermost shell has five, six, or seven electrons, the atom finds it easier to gain or share electrons to reach the stable octet of eight, so the valency is eight minus that count, as in oxygen with 2, 6 giving valency 2 or nitrogen with 2, 5 giving valency 3. The first twenty elements are the practice ground for this: hydrogen is 1 and has valency 1, helium 2 and valency 0, lithium 2,1 and valency 1, beryllium 2,2 and valency 2, boron 2,3 and valency 3, carbon 2,4 and valency 4, nitrogen 2,5 and valency 3, oxygen 2,6 and valency 2, fluorine 2,7 and valency 1, neon 2,8 and valency 0, and so on through sodium, magnesium, aluminium, silicon, phosphorus, sulphur, chlorine, argon, potassium, and calcium. Molecules of elements such as O2, N2 and H2 form when two like atoms share electrons so that each attains a stable or stable-like configuration, while molecules of compounds such as H2O, CO2, NO2, CaO and ZnCl2 form when atoms of different elements combine in fixed ratios determined by their valencies. The octet rule, the tendency of atoms to have eight electrons in the outermost shell, is the guiding force, and a stable octet explains why noble gases like neon and argon show valency 0.
textWalkthrough:
Remember, in Class 7 you already met valency as the combining capacity of an element. You learned that the electronic configuration could be read to find how many electrons were in the outermost shell, and that number gave you a clue to how an atom would behave. That was the seed planted in the DEPTH_PREREQ node c7_chem_011. Now, in Class 8, we water that seed with the PREREQ node c8_chem_006, where you met Bohr's shell model. Bohr told us that electrons do not wander anywhere; they stay in fixed energy levels or shells around the nucleus. Why does that matter? Because the shell model is the reason the outermost shell electrons are the ones that decide valency and, therefore, how molecules and compounds are formed.

Let us walk through the idea slowly, as if we are solving a puzzle together. Imagine you are filling seats in a bus. The first row, the K-shell, has only two seats. The second row, the L-shell, has eight. For the first twenty elements, the third row, M-shell, also has eight, and the fourth row, N-shell, begins to take passengers from potassium onward. Electrons, like passengers, fill the front rows before moving to the back. So hydrogen, with one electron, has configuration 1. Helium, with two, fills the K-shell and becomes 2. Lithium, with three, has two in K and one in L, written 2,1. Beryllium is 2,2, boron 2,3, carbon 2,4, nitrogen 2,5, oxygen 2,6, fluorine 2,7, neon 2,8. After neon the M-shell begins: sodium is 2,8,1, magnesium 2,8,2, and so on up to argon 2,8,8, and then potassium and calcium put one and two electrons in the N-shell.

Now, which of these passengers decides where the atom goes? Only the ones in the last occupied row, the outermost shell or valence shell. That is where valency lives. If the last shell has one, two, three, or four electrons, the atom behaves like a hand holding out those electrons to grasp others; sodium has one finger open, so it can clasp one electron from another atom, giving valency 1. Carbon has four fingers open, so it can form four bonds, giving valency 4. If the last shell has five, six, or seven electrons, it is easier for the atom to receive or share the few missing ones to reach the stable octet. Thus oxygen, with six, needs only two more, giving valency 2; fluorine, with seven, needs one more, giving valency 1. And when the last shell is already full, like neon with 2,8, the atom has no open fingers; the parking lot is full, so valency is 0.

Let us see what a good answer looks like versus a weak one. If the question asks, "Write the electronic configuration of sulphur and state its valency," a good answer says: "Sulphur has atomic number 16, so its electronic configuration is 2,8,6. The outermost shell has six electrons, so it needs two more to complete the octet; therefore its valency is 2." A weak answer says: "Sulphur is 2,8,6 and its valency is 6." That answer has the configuration right but the valency wrong, because it does not compare the six outer electrons with the stable octet. Always ask: is the outermost shell closer to being empty or full?

Now connect this to real molecules. Oxygen, 2,6, has two open fingers; two oxygen atoms can each share two fingers with each other, giving the O2 molecule. Hydrogen, with one electron, can share one finger; two hydrogen atoms share to form H2. Water forms because oxygen shares one finger with each of two hydrogen atoms, so each H reaches a duet and O reaches an octet. Carbon dioxide forms because carbon, 2,4, shares four fingers in total, two with each oxygen, making CO2. Ionic compounds such as CaO and ZnCl2 form because calcium can give its two outer electrons and oxygen accepts them, while zinc gives two and each chlorine accepts one. The point is that the valency tells you how many puzzle pieces each atom can connect.

In the ICSE board exam, expect either a direct recall question such as "Write the electronic configuration of sodium and find its valency," or a reasoning question such as "Why is neon unreactive?" The examiner wants to see the link between the outermost shell and the stable octet, not just a memorised number. Show the configuration, point to the outermost shell, and then use that to explain the valency or the molecule that forms.

The last layer, the outermost shell, tells us how many friends the atom can hold hands with; that number is called valency. If the outer shell is full like neon, the atom does not want any more friends.
misconceptionText:
1. "Valency is just the number of electrons in the last shell." This is one of the most persistent errors. The board examiner has repeatedly noted that candidates write electronic configurations without explaining how the number relates to the stable octet. For example, a student writes oxygen as 2,6 and then says its valency is 6. The correction is: for more than four electrons in the outermost shell, valency is eight minus that number, because the atom gains or shares the missing electrons to complete the octet. So oxygen, 2,6, has valency 2, not 6.

2. "A full outermost shell always contains eight electrons." This confuses the stable octet with the K-shell exception. board examiner observations about candidates being unsure of hydrogen and small atoms remind us that the K-shell is full with only two electrons. Hydrogen has configuration 1 and valency 1; helium has 2 and valency 0. For the first period, stability means two electrons, not eight. The correction is to check which shell is being filled: the K-shell holds 2, the L-shell 8, and the M-shell 8 for the first twenty elements.

3. "Elements with the same number of outer electrons always form the same kind of compound." board exam guidance on covalent versus ionic compounds show that students sometimes pick NaCl as the formula for a covalent substance or fail to recognise CCl4 as covalent. The correction is that valency tells you the combining ratio, but the type of bond depends on how the atoms share or transfer electrons. O2 and H2 are molecules of elements sharing electrons, while H2O and CO2 are molecules of compounds, and CaO and ZnCl2 are ionic compounds in which electrons have been transferred.

Q1 (recall): Write the electronic configuration of the following elements: sodium, carbon, neon, and chlorine. Also state the valency of each.
Answer: Sodium has atomic number 11, so its electronic configuration is 2,8,1. The outermost shell has one electron, which it can lose, so its valency is 1. Carbon has atomic number 6, so its electronic configuration is 2,4. The outermost shell has four electrons, and carbon can share all four, so its valency is 4. Neon has atomic number 10, so its electronic configuration is 2,8. The outermost shell is already full, giving it a stable octet, so its valency is 0. Chlorine has atomic number 17, so its electronic configuration is 2,8,7. The outermost shell has seven electrons, so it needs one more to complete the octet; therefore its valency is 1. Remembering this pattern is the foundation for everything else in this node.

Q2 (reasoning): Why does oxygen have a valency of 2, while nitrogen has a valency of 3?
Answer: Oxygen has atomic number 8 and its electronic configuration is 2,6. Its outermost shell, the L-shell, contains six electrons. To reach the stable octet of eight electrons, oxygen can gain or share two more electrons; therefore its valency is 2. Nitrogen has atomic number 7 and its electronic configuration is 2,5. Its outermost shell contains five electrons, so it can gain or share three more electrons to complete the octet; therefore its valency is 3. The difference is not a rule to be memorised blindly but a consequence of counting how many electrons are missing from eight. An atom tends to choose the path that requires the least effort, and for oxygen that is two electrons, for nitrogen three.

Q3 (evaluate): A student claims: "The valency of an element is always equal to the number of electrons in its outermost shell." Evaluate this statement with suitable examples.
Answer: This statement is only partly true. It is true when the outermost shell has one, two, three, or four electrons because the atom can readily lose or share that many electrons. For example, sodium with 2,8,1 has one electron in its outermost shell and valency 1; magnesium with 2,8,2 has two electrons and valency 2; boron with 2,3 has three and valency 3; carbon with 2,4 has four and valency 4. However, the statement is false when the outermost shell has more than four electrons. In those cases the atom prefers to gain or share the missing electrons to complete the stable octet of eight, so the valency is eight minus the number of outermost electrons. For example, nitrogen with 2,5 has five outer electrons but valency 3, because 8 minus 5 equals 3; oxygen with 2,6 has valency 2, because 8 minus 6 equals 2; fluorine with 2,7 has valency 1, because 8 minus 7 equals 1. The statement also fails for noble gases such as neon with 2,8: it has eight outer electrons but valency 0, because it already has a stable octet and does not need to combine. Therefore, the relationship between outermost-shell electrons and valency depends on whether the shell is closer to being empty or full, and a balanced view requires considering both the direct count for one to four outer electrons and the "eight minus" rule for five to seven.

Q4 (apply): The electronic configuration of magnesium is 2,8,2 and that of oxygen is 2,6. Predict the formula of the compound formed between magnesium and oxygen, and explain how the transfer of electrons leads to a stable compound.
Answer: Magnesium has two electrons in its outermost shell, so it can lose two electrons and reach the stable configuration 2,8. Oxygen has six electrons in its outermost shell, so it can gain two electrons and reach the stable octet 2,8. When magnesium and oxygen combine, one magnesium atom transfers its two outermost electrons to one oxygen atom. The magnesium becomes Mg2+ and the oxygen becomes O2-. These oppositely charged ions attract each other strongly and form the ionic compound magnesium oxide with formula MgO. The formula is MgO because one Mg2+ ion exactly balances one O2- ion; the two plus and two minus charges cancel. This example shows how the valencies, 2 for magnesium and 2 for oxygen, determine the 1:1 ratio in the compound and how both atoms achieve stable configurations.

Q5 (create): Imagine you are designing a board game called "Valency Quest" for Class 8 students. In this game each player picks an atom card showing the electronic configuration of one of the first twenty elements. Design one round of the game in which players must use their cards to form the molecules O2, H2O and NaCl. Explain the rules a player must follow to decide which cards can bond and how many bonds each card can make.
Answer: In "Valency Quest", each atom card displays the name, atomic number and electronic configuration of an element such as hydrogen 1, oxygen 2,6, sodium 2,8,1 or chlorine 2,8,7. The first rule is that every player must look at the outermost shell of their card and use the octet rule to decide how many electrons the atom wants to gain, lose or share; that number is the valency or the number of bonds the card can make. For the O2 round, a player holding an oxygen card sees six outer electrons and a valency of 2, so two oxygen cards can share two pairs of electrons, forming a double bond between them. For the H2O round, one oxygen card with valency 2 bonds with two hydrogen cards, each with valency 1; the oxygen shares one pair with each hydrogen, giving all atoms stable outer shells. For the NaCl round, a sodium card has one outer electron that it can transfer to a chlorine card, which has seven outer electrons and needs one more. The sodium becomes Na+ and the chlorine becomes Cl-, and the two cards lock together as NaCl. A successful player must state the electronic configuration, count the outermost shell electrons, decide the valency, and then justify the number and type of bonds. The winner is the player who forms the most correct molecules and can explain why each combination is stable.

title: Language of chemistry - valency and formulae
definition: Valency is the combining capacity of an element, the fixed number of bonds or equivalents an atom of that element can form when it joins with atoms of other elements to make a compound. It is the single most useful number for a beginner chemist, because once the valencies of two combining elements are known, the correct molecular formula of a binary compound can be written without guessing. A molecular formula is a shorthand way of showing which elements are present in a compound and in what numerical ratio, with the small numbers called subscripts telling us how many atoms of each element are present in one molecule or one formula unit of the substance. The first twenty elements have their own one- or two-letter chemical symbols, which act as a shorthand notation for the full names; for example, H for hydrogen, He for helium, Li for lithium, Be for beryllium, B for boron, C for carbon, N for nitrogen, O for oxygen, F for fluorine, Ne for neon, Na for sodium, Mg for magnesium, Al for aluminium, Si for silicon, P for phosphorus, S for sulphur, Cl for chlorine, Ar for argon, K for potassium and Ca for calcium. Many of these symbols come from the Latin or other historical names of the elements, so the symbol does not always match the modern English name; Na comes from natrium, K from kalium, Fe from ferrum, Cu from cuprum, Ag from argentum, Au from aurum and Hg from hydrargyrum. To write the formula of a simple compound using the criss-cross method, the valencies of the two combining elements are swapped across as subscripts, giving the simplest whole number ratio of atoms that satisfies each other's combining capacity. For example, sodium has valency one and chlorine has valency one, so the one crosses to Na1 and the other to Cl1, and the final molecular formula is written NaCl. Magnesium has valency two and chlorine has valency one, so the two becomes the subscript of chlorine and the one becomes the subscript of magnesium, giving MgCl2. When both elements have the same valency, such as calcium with valency two and oxygen with valency two, the numbers cancel down to one each, producing CaO rather than Ca2O2. This is because a formula must always show the simplest fixed proportion of atoms, and the subscripts are reduced to the lowest whole number ratio just like a fraction in mathematics. The criss-cross method therefore turns the abstract idea of combining capacity into a practical rule for formula writing, and it is the bridge between knowing the symbol of an element and expressing a compound in the concise, universal language of chemistry.
textWalkthrough:
Welcome back to the language of chemistry. Before this node, in c7_chem_011, you learned that valency is the combining capacity of an element and that it is linked to the arrangement of electrons in the outermost shell of an atom. In c8_chem_007 you saw how the electronic configuration of an element determines its valency, so by now you already carry the most important tool in your pocket: the valency number. This node is about taking that number and using it to write the correct molecular formula of a compound. The whole process is like a recipe: once you know the ingredients and the exact amounts in which they combine, you can write the finished dish in a short, coded form.

Let us begin with the simplest building blocks, the symbols of the first twenty elements. Think of a chemical symbol as a nickname, a shorthand that every chemist in the world recognises. Just as the country code on a number plate tells you where a vehicle is registered in just a few letters, a symbol like Na for sodium or Ca for calcium tells a chemist the element instantly. Do not be troubled when the symbol does not look like the English name; many were chosen from older names because scientists across different countries agreed on them long ago. Write the names and symbols side by side until the one-to-one link feels automatic: H, He, Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Ne, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar, K, Ca.

Now for the central idea. Suppose one atom of element A can hold hands with one atom of element B. We say each has a combining capacity, or valency, of one. The simplest ratio in which they combine is one to one, and the formula is AB. That is exactly what happens in sodium chloride, common salt, where Na has valency one and Cl has valency one, giving the familiar formula NaCl. But what if the two atoms do not have the same combining capacity? Magnesium, with two hands free, needs two chlorine atoms, each with one hand free, to use up all its combining power. If we simply write MgCl, we are hiding the fact that one magnesium atom must combine with two chlorine atoms. The correct formula is MgCl2, where the small subscript 2 after Cl tells us the number of chlorine atoms.

This is where the criss-cross method comes in. Imagine you are crossing the laces of your shoes to make a firm knot. Write the symbols in a line, put the valency of each element above its symbol, then swap the numbers down as subscripts on the other element. For magnesium chloride, Mg has valency 2 and Cl has valency 1. After the criss-cross, the 2 of Mg becomes the subscript of Cl, and the 1 of Cl becomes the subscript of Mg. This gives MgCl2. For calcium oxide, Ca has valency 2 and O has valency 2. After crossing, you would get Ca2O2, but a molecular formula must be in the simplest whole number ratio, so you divide both by 2 to get CaO. For water, H has valency 1 and O has valency 2. The 2 drops to H and the 1 to O, giving H2O. Notice how the tiny subscript 2 in H2O is not the number of oxygens; it is the number of hydrogens. A bad answer would be HO2, because that would put the wrong number on the wrong element, just as putting your left shoe on your right foot feels uncomfortable.

Let us compare good and bad answers. Good: writing Al2O3 for aluminium oxide because Al has valency 3 and O has valency 2, the 3 crosses to O and the 2 crosses to Al. Bad: writing AlO or Al3O2, which either ignores the difference in combining capacity or fails to reduce the ratio. Good: reducing Cu2O2 to Cu2O for copper(I) oxide once the valencies are known. Bad: leaving Cu2O2 as it is, which is not the simplest ratio. Good: treating a formula as a ratio, not a price tag, so CaCl2 means one calcium atom for every two chlorine atoms. Bad: reading CaCl2 as "one calcium and two chlorines only," forgetting that the formula represents a large, repeating structure in the solid.

The board examiner observations that we have been given remind us that students often lose marks through notation and formula confusion. Examiners have reported that some candidates wrote a molecular formula when they were asked for a name or a structure, and others used wrong notation for elements or confused covalent and ionic examples. In this topic, the most common notation slip is writing the subscript in the wrong place, such as H2Cl instead of HCl, or failing to reduce the formula to its simplest form. Always look back at the subscript after you have crossed the valencies and ask: can both numbers be divided by the same whole number? If yes, reduce them.

As you prepare for the board exam, expect short questions in which you are given the valencies of two elements and asked to write the molecular formula, or in which you are shown a formula and asked to decide whether the valencies have been used correctly. The examiner wants to see the correct use of the criss-cross method, the correct placement of subscripts, and the ability to recall the symbols of the first twenty elements. Practice by covering the formula column of a table and writing the formula from the symbol and valency alone. When the criss-cross becomes a quick, automatic movement, you will have mastered the language of chemistry at this stage.
